summary:
Benue State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide: it was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, and it makes entering a same-sex marriage or civil union liable to 14 years' imprisonment, while registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, is liable to 10 years. The Act also reaches people who help arrange same-sex weddings and those who attend them.

Criminal exposure in Benue is set by the federal maximum rather than by Shari'a law. Twelve Shari'a-administering states impose harsher penalties for same-sex conduct, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism; Benue is not among them, so the applicable ceiling for same-sex conduct is the federal 14-year term. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

A 2022 court ruling narrowed part of this regime. A coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a judgment that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, which effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. No comparable ruling is recorded for the conduct-provisions or the marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain in force.

The Constitution contains no specific protections on the basis of sexual orientation, and there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Visitors therefore have no statutory complaint route if they are targeted.

Entry and transit screening carries documented risk. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated Nigeria travel advice, as reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, states that same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and notes that some states under Shari'a law can prescribe the death penalty.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed in practice. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged. Police violence against perceived gay people is also routine: in March 2025 Lagos police struck a 24-year-old man in the mouth with a gun butt and released him only after he paid part of a 50,000 naira bribe, for looking gay.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), who pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, and served it in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion; an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Visitors who use dating apps face a documented entrapment pattern. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) records kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Human Rights Watch reported in October 2016 that police have used the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests, and those affected describe the law as weaponised, producing a climate of hostility independent of its text. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are reported as common, especially in the Shari'a states.

Transgender Nigerians have also lived since at least September 2022 under the shadow of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Compared with the twelve Shari'a-administering states, where male sodomy can carry death under state Zina provisions, Benue's exposure is lower but not absent: the federal 14-year maximum and the Criminal Code provisions still apply in full.
localsOnly:
Residents of Benue face the same statutory ceilings as visitors: 14 years for entering a same-sex marriage or civil union, 10 years for registering, operating or participating in a gay club, society or organisation or for a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, up to 14 years for sex between men under the Criminal Code, and up to 3 years for gross indecency.

The 2022 constitutional ruling has practical consequences for resident organising: because Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) were held unenforceable nationwide, LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals can exist and organise under those sections, while the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions remain enforceable.

Residents have no federal anti-discrimination protection and no constitutional protection on grounds of sexual orientation, so employment, housing and service disputes grounded in perceived sexual orientation or gender identity have no statutory remedy.

Placement of transgender prisoners between male and female sections is left to the discretion of the Nigerian Correctional Service; the October 2024 panel found that at least one such placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, but no general policy is recorded in these sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Rights Watch country page for Nigeria yielded no usable source finding specific to Benue in this inventory; the state-level picture here rests on the national statute, the Criminal Code and the 2022 constitutional ruling rather than on Benue-specific reporting.

Whether the 2022 judgment has been appealed, narrowed or complied with in Benue's courts is unresolved in the sources available here.

Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted into law is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Benue-specific enforcement data — arrest figures, police directives or local prosecutions under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act — is recorded in this inventory.
